name: monad
intent: Give a computation's effect (absence, failure, asynchrony, I/O, state) a type of its own with a unit and a bind operation, so that a sequence of steps in which each step depends on the previous value composes into one pipeline while bind propagates the effect automatically.
problem: Sequencing computations where the next step needs the previous step's result and every step may additionally be absent, failing, asynchronous or effectful pushes the effect handling into the business logic: nested null checks, try/catch ladders, callback pyramids. Every call site repeats the same propagation decision (short-circuit? await? log?) and one forgotten check turns a controlled failure into a crash or a wrong value.
context: Applies wherever a value and the fact that it is absent, pending, failing or impure belong together: chained lookups, validation and error pipelines, asynchronous call chains, state threading, parser and interpreter pipelines, and effect-typed application cores. It matters most when the sequence is long, when the effect policy must be uniform and testable, and when the language already provides monadic types (Optional, Result, Promise, IO) or syntax that desugars to bind (do-notation, for-comprehensions, async/await).
benefits: Dependent steps compose without ad-hoc control flow: bind injects the short-circuit/await/propagation rule once, so each step stays a total function a -> M b instead of a nest of guards.
The effect becomes a replaceable value: swapping Maybe for Either, or a synchronous result for an asynchronous one, changes the type and the interpreter, not the shape of every call site.
Testability and equational reasoning: steps are pure and the effect is data, so pipelines can be built, inspected and property-tested (the three monad laws) before anything is executed.
Uniform failure semantics: absence, failure and ordering are explicit in the types, so 'what happens when a step fails' is decided once, inside bind.
The pattern names what several language features already desugar to (do-notation, C# query expressions, Scala for-comprehensions, async/await, Rust's ?), which unifies vocabulary a team uses daily.
tradeoffs: Comprehension tax: the bind signature and its vocabulary (functor, applicative, Kleisli) are famously hard to teach, and half-adopted monads are worse than explicit imperative code.
Effects do not compose freely: combining async with error handling, logging or state needs monad transformers, an effect stack or an effect system, which multiplies types and ceremony.

Allocation and deferred execution: each bind wraps a value and a closure and postpones work, which costs in hot paths (Rust's null-pointer optimization and native async/await mitigate it; hand-rolled boxes do not).

Debugging shifts: stack traces cross lambda and interpreter boundaries, lazy descriptions execute far from their definition, and step-through tooling shows the monad's interpreter rather than the business step.
Effect creep and escape hatches: one effect tends to colonise every signature ('IO everywhere'), while get/unwrap/unsafeRun concentrate the risk exactly where the discipline is dropped.

participants.responsibility: The effect-carrying type: it maps a value type a to the type M a of computations over it (Maybe, Either, Result, Promise, Future, IO, List, State) and defines what 'a value plus an effect' means.
Injects a plain value into the monadic type without adding an effect, giving the pipeline its identity element and letting total functions enter the context.

Takes a monadic value and a step function a -> M b, applies the effect-specific policy (propagate absence, short-circuit on failure, await completion, thread state) and flattens the result back to M b, so dependent steps form one chain.
The per-step computation a -> M b; it carries the business logic and returns the effect explicitly instead of performing it.
The instance-specific constructors of effects (fail/none, putStrLn, async, get/put) plus the runner that finally executes the description (unsafeRun, await, collect, runState) at the program edge.

use_cases: Chained lookups where any link may be missing: user -> address -> city expressed with Maybe/Optional instead of nested null checks.
Validation and error pipelines in which each step can fail with a domain error and the first failure must short-circuit (Either/Result, railway-oriented programming).
Asynchronous workflows whose next call depends on the previous response (Promise/async-await, CompletableFuture.thenCompose, Kotlin suspend functions, Swift Task).
Effect description and interpretation: building an IO/program value that is pure data and running it through different interpreters in tests and production (IO monad, tagless-final).
State-threading computations such as compiler passes, random generators or incremental traversals written as a State monad pipeline.
Parser combinators and nondeterministic search, where each step consumes the previous parse result or explores every value produced by the previous step (parser monad, List monad).
Rust's std::result::Result composes fallible steps with and_then and the ? operator, returning early on Err while keeping the successful value available to the next dependent step.
Java's CompletableFuture.thenCompose chains dependent asynchronous stages: the function returns another CompletionStage and the outer stage adopts its completion or exceptional failure.

Scala for-comprehensions over Option, collections, or other types with map, flatMap, and withFilter desugar dependent bindings into the corresponding combinators, keeping the monadic sequence readable without hiding its operations.
avoid_when: The effects are independent: use applicative/parallel combination (Promise.all, asyncio.gather, traverse, Task.WhenAll) instead of bind, which serialises work that could run concurrently.
A single presence or error check is all that is needed: guard clauses, a null object or a default value, or one try/catch are simpler and clearer.

The host language already makes the sequence linear and safe (exceptions, await, explicit error returns) and no effect policy needs abstracting - a hand-written monad adds ceremony without new guarantees.
The code is a hot inner loop where wrapper allocation, closures or boxing dominate the work; keep the effect at the edges and the loop imperative.
The team has no functional background and no library providing the monad: introducing the vocabulary without a real effect boundary yields inconsistent, half-monadic code.
anti_patterns: 'Monadic everything': wrapping every value in Maybe/IO until signatures stop carrying business meaning and the effect vocabulary colonises the codebase.
Hand-rolled Either/promise containers as a style statement in languages whose idiom is exceptions or error returns, leaving two competing error channels.
Law-breaking instances: a bind that runs eagerly, mutates its context or is not associative, so refactoring a chain (or letting the compiler desugar it) changes behaviour.
Deep bind/then nesting of independent effects instead of applicative combination, serialising work that had no dependency.
Using a Reader or State monad as an ad-hoc dependency-injection or config-passing mechanism instead of the effect it is meant to model.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: step logic (what) is separate from effect handling (how and when), which lives in bind and the interpreter.
Composition over control flow: small total functions a -> M b compose into pipelines instead of nested guards and callbacks.
Equational reasoning: the monad laws make chained and factored forms equivalent, so mechanical transformations preserve behaviour.
Parametricity and reuse: one generic bind serves every instance (Maybe, Either, Future, IO, List, State).
Dependency inversion: steps depend on the abstract operations rather than a concrete runtime, which makes the interpreter (production vs test) replaceable.
best_practices: Keep the effect at the type level: step functions return M b, and unwrapping (get/unwrap/unsafeRun) happens only at the program edge.
Prefer monads the language already ships (Optional, Result, Promise, Task, Future) or its desugaring syntax (async/await, for-comprehensions, query expressions) over hand-rolled containers.
Implement and test the instance before the pipeline: pure/unit, bind, the effect primitives, and the three laws as property tests.
Pick the weakest effect that models the problem (Maybe before Either before IO) and keep transformers to a minimum by extracting pure logic out of the effect stack.
Model independence explicitly: map/filter/traverse (applicative) for steps that do not consume the previous value, bind only for genuine dependency.
Write one interpreter per environment (production, test, replay) and keep failure information in the typed error channel instead of logging it away.
sources: Moggi, Notions of computation and monads, Information and Computation 93(1), 1991 - introduced monads as the semantics of computational effects.
Wadler, Monads for functional programming, Advanced Functional Programming (LNCS 925), 1995 - the tutorial that made the pattern practical.
Gibbons & Oliveira, The Essence of the Iterator Pattern (2006) - monads and applicatives as composable design vocabulary.
